property_summary: Calling sendTo from this contract should only succeed (not revert) when this contract is the recorded owner; non-owner callers must be unable to trigger the transfer.
Only the contract owner is allowed to successfully call sendTo (i.e., calls from non-owner addresses always revert).

If calling c.sendTo from this test does not revert, then the call must have reverted equivalently to (msg.sender != msg.sender) — i.e., the test's original asserted relation between reverted and caller must hold.
If the call to c.sendTo does not revert then the boolean 'reverted' must equal (msg.sender != msg.sender) (i.e., the existing assert remains unchanged).
If the call to c.sendTo does NOT revert then the boolean 'reverted' must equal (msg.sender != msg.sender).

For all callers and amounts, the reference contract allows the owner to successfully call sendTo (call does not revert and may transfer), whereas the mutant rejects calls from the owner (require(msg.sender != owner)), so there exists inputs (caller == owner) that make the mutant revert while the reference accepts them.

For any caller who is the owner and any receiver/address and amount, calling sendTo transfers funds out of the contract to the provided receiver (so address(c).balance decreases by amount and receiver's balance increases accordingly); the mutant sends to msg.sender instead, violating this for inputs where owner != receiver and amount > 0.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any nonzero amount, after calling sendTo(receiver, amount) the reference contract always decreases address(c).balance by amount and increases the specified receiver's balance by amount; the mutant instead sends to msg.sender, so when owner != receiver and amount>0 the receiver's balance does not increase by amount (the property that receiver's balance increases by amount is violated).

For any caller who is the owner and any positive amount up to the contract balance, after sendTo(receiver, amount) executes the contract's balance decreases by exactly amount (i.e., funds are forwarded out of the contract); the mutant that always transfers to owner can violate observed recipient balances because the contract still loses funds but the intended recipient does not receive them, so reading address(c).balance alone distinguishes behaviors when recipient != owner.
